content.sample_usage_scenario: A data engineering team needs to enforce that a generated batch_number column (used by downstream reconciliation logic) always contains even integers after daily ETL loads across multiple production tables with millions of rows. A reusable dbt generic test is the optimal approach so the same validation can be referenced in schema YAML for many models/sources and included in CI to fail builds when odd values are introduced.
content.key_considerations: Ensure the tested column is an integer type (or cast it) and decide how to handle NULLs; on very large tables the mod operation will scan rows—consider running this test on partitioned / recent partitions or as part of incremental checks to reduce cost and run-time. Also set an appropriate dbt test severity and include the test in schema.yml for maintainability.

content.sample_usage_scenario: A data engineering team building a dbt project needs to enforce data quality rules that prevent empty strings in critical customer-facing text columns (e.g., email, first_name, product_description). The requirement is to add a clear, documented, reusable test that can be applied across many models and surfaced in dbt docs so analysts and engineers can quickly see which columns are failing this rule during CI runs and nightly checks.
content.code_for_scenario:
macros:  
  - name: test_not_empty_string  
    description: Complementary test to default `not_null` test as it checks that there is not an empty string. It only accepts columns of type string.  
    arguments:  
      - name: model   
        type: string  
        description: Model Name  
      - name: column_name  
        type: string  
        description: Column name that should not be an empty string
content.key_considerations: Ensure the test macro implementation enforces both NOT NULL and != '' (empty string) semantics and is executed efficiently (e.g., using WHERE clauses or leveraging indexable predicates). Document its use in dbt schema.yml clearly and validate column data types before applying the test; on very large tables consider running as a sampled/filtered check during development and full checks in scheduled CI to manage run-time and cost.

content.sample_usage_scenario: You maintain a dbt project for a data warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift) where staging tables are populated from upstream sources and must reference canonical dimension tables (e.g., customer_id referencing dim_customers). Before production deployments, you need a reusable test that flags any child rows with a non-null foreign key that has no matching parent row, at data volumes of tens of millions of rows where a simple ad-hoc query would be costly and hard to reproduce across environments.
content.key_considerations: For very large tables, avoid anti-joins expressed with NOT IN due to performance and NULL semantics—consider rewriting as a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE parent.id IS NULL or leveraging hashed keys; ensure the test runs in CI incremental contexts to limit compute costs and that the dbt user has read access to both schemas. Also consider that many cloud warehouses do not enforce foreign keys, so this test is an application-level integrity check and will incur query costs when run frequently.

content.sample_usage_scenario: A payments analytics team needs an automated way to warn when numeric identifier columns (e.g., transaction_id or invoice_number) contain odd values, because downstream matching logic requires even IDs for reconciliation. The data warehouse receives millions of rows per day, and the team wants a reusable dbt generic test that can be applied to multiple models/columns; alternatives include custom SQL checks run in orchestration or embedding checks in the ELT job, but a dbt generic test is optimal for reusability and integration with the model test framework.
content.key_considerations: Be aware of database-specific modulus behavior and SQL dialect differences (e.g., some warehouses use MOD(column, 2) instead of %), and ensure the tested column is numeric or safely cast to an integer to avoid runtime errors. For large tables, returning full rows can be expensive—limit results or sample when needed, and consider writing targeted assertions (count > 0) or adding filters (recent partition) to reduce cost and runtime.

content.sample_usage_scenario: A data engineering team maintains a dbt project that enforces uniqueness on user emails across several large, rapidly-updating source tables. The business requires that soft-deleted users (is_deleted = true) be ignored when checking uniqueness and that email comparisons be case-insensitive, so they need to override dbt's built-in unique test with a project-local implementation that applies these domain-specific rules.
content.code_for_scenario:
{% test unique(model, column_name) %}
  -- Project-local override of dbt's builtin `unique` generic test.
  -- This implementation ignores soft-deleted rows and treats emails case-insensitively.
  -- Place this file at: tests/generic/unique.sql

  SELECT
    lower({{ column_name }}) AS violating_value,
    COUNT(*) AS occurrences
  FROM {{ model }}
  WHERE coalesce(is_deleted, false) = false
    AND {{ column_name }} IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
{% endtest %}
content.key_considerations: Overriding a built-in test means your project takes ownership of that behavior—document it and review on dbt upgrades. For very large tables, the GROUP BY can be expensive; consider running this test on incremental snapshots or on partitioned subsets, and ensure appropriate indexes exist (e.g., lower(email) or a normalized email column) to reduce scan cost.
